blocks.text: The operations on a 2D array mirror the 1D list, with one addition that dominates real code: you often need to visit every cell, and there is more than one order in which to do it.

blocks.code:
const mark = marks[1][2];   // read
marks[1][2] = 65;           // write

blocks.text: Both are **O(1)**. Two index computations instead of one, but neither depends on the size of the grid.
This is the workhorse. Two nested loops, outer over rows, inner over columns:

A grid of R rows and C columns holds R x C cells, so a full sweep costs **O(R x C)**. If the grid is square with side N, that is O(N²) — which is why nested loops over a grid are the classic example of quadratic time.
The cost is unavoidable when you genuinely need every cell. What you *can* control is the order, and that turns out to matter more than most people expect.
These two look symmetrical and are not:

items: **Read one row** — O(C). The cells sit next to each other in memory.
**Read one column** — O(R). The cells are scattered, one row-length apart.

blocks.text: Both touch the same number of cells for a square grid, yet reading a column is reliably slower on real hardware. The reason is the subject of the next lesson, and it is the most practically useful idea in this chapter.

Adding a row or column is expensive — **O(R x C)** in the worst case — because the no-gaps rule still applies. Inserting a column means every single row has to shift its contents. For that reason, grids are usually built once at a fixed size rather than grown.
